sections.title: Abraham had nothing to boast about
sections.line: Credited, not earned — the wage-versus-gift distinction does the work.

sections.title: David says the same thing
sections.line: A second witness, and this one speaks of sin not counted.

sections.title: Before circumcision, not after
sections.line: The timing is the argument: faith came first, so Gentiles are included.

sections.title: Promise, not law
sections.line: Law can only bring wrath; a promise can rest on grace.

sections.title: Faith against the evidence
sections.line: Two dead bodies, one promise, and Abraham believes anyway.

sections.title: Written for us
sections.line: The Genesis sentence was always aimed past Abraham at the reader.

themes.note: A bookkeeping word, repeated until the accounting is unmistakable.
Sequence is the proof: the sign came after the righteousness.
Abraham widens from one nation's ancestor to everyone who believes.
A promise rests on grace, so it can actually be guaranteed.

references.why: The verse the whole chapter turns on — Paul reads 'credited' as accounting language and builds the case on it.
Brings David in as a second witness, and states the same thing negatively: sin not counted.
God renamed Abraham father of many nations before he had a son, so the promise always outran the evidence.
The stars promise, cited to show what Abraham was believing against a hundred-year-old body.

purpose: Paul wants us to know Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, so that Gentile believers are not second-tier children.
He wants us to believe righteousness is credited rather than earned, because a wage can be claimed but a gift can only be received.
He wants us to read Genesis as written for us, so that the same faith that answered a dead womb can answer an empty tomb.
